# AML evidence packet — draft v1

This curated input is not a comprehensive review. Every method receives the same UTF-8 file. Summaries are original paraphrases. Bibliographic metadata and abstracts were checked through the public NCBI ID converter and PubMed EFetch on 2026-10-05. Selected studies predate 2025. Co-Scientist's validated candidates and generated proposals are not input or the only correct answers.

## Research question

Propose one mechanistically specific AML drug-repurposing hypothesis using a drug approved for a different indication. Specify the biological context, supported premises and speculative bridges, selectivity and translational limitations, and a discriminating preclinical validation strategy with a falsifying outcome. State the original indication and distinguish verified facts from prior knowledge that needs checking. Do not present an established AML regimen as a new repurposing discovery. This adapts the Co-Scientist objective rather than reproducing a private original prompt.

## S1 — A leukemia-stem-cell metabolic dependency

Lagadinou et al. (2013), *BCL-2 inhibition targets oxidative phosphorylation and selectively eradicates quiescent human leukemia stem cells*. Cell Stem Cell. DOI: `10.1016/j.stem.2012.12.013`; PMID: `23333149`; PMCID: `PMC3595363`. [Primary record](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/23333149/).

Functionally defined leukemia stem cells in the studied specimens frequently had low reactive-oxygen-species levels and elevated BCL-2. BCL-2 inhibition reduced oxidative phosphorylation and affected quiescent leukemia stem cells. This motivates investigating specific dependencies and selectivity. It does not establish that an arbitrary mitochondrial inhibitor has an acceptable therapeutic window or works across every AML context.

## S2 — Resistant cells are not necessarily the same stem-cell population

Farge et al. (2017), *Chemotherapy-Resistant Human Acute Myeloid Leukemia Cells Are Not Enriched for Leukemic Stem Cells but Require Oxidative Metabolism*. Cancer Discovery. DOI: `10.1158/2159-8290.CD-16-0441`; PMID: `28416471`; PMCID: `PMC5501738`. [Primary record](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/28416471/).

Residual cells in cytarabine-treated models were not consistently enriched for immature, quiescent leukemia stem cells. They displayed oxidative-metabolism-associated properties, including mitochondrial and fatty-acid-oxidation-related features. Altering that state changed treatment response in the studied settings. This cautions against equating all residual disease with the ROS-low population in S1. These model findings do not establish clinical efficacy of a new compound.

## S3 — An established mechanistic comparator

Pollyea et al. (2018), *Venetoclax with azacitidine disrupts energy metabolism and targets leukemia stem cells in patients with acute myeloid leukemia*. Nature Medicine. DOI: `10.1038/s41591-018-0233-1`; PMID: `30420752`; PMCID: `PMC7001730`. [Primary record](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/30420752/).

The report connected venetoclax–azacitidine treatment to changes in leukemia-stem-cell energy metabolism, including TCA-cycle and oxidative-phosphorylation effects, using patient-associated observations and experimental follow-up. It provides an established comparator. Repeating this combination is not a new repurposing proposal. The findings cannot be transferred directly to another drug or treated as universal randomized comparative efficacy evidence.

## S4 — Differentiation as a distinct outcome

Sykes et al. (2016), *Inhibition of Dihydroorotate Dehydrogenase Overcomes Differentiation Blockade in Acute Myeloid Leukemia*. Cell. DOI: `10.1016/j.cell.2016.08.057`; PMID: `27641501`; PMCID: `PMC7360335`. [Primary record](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/27641501/).

DHODH inhibition promoted myeloid differentiation in experimental AML systems and affected disease-related endpoints in the investigated models. This connects metabolism with differentiation and supplies an alternative to nonspecific cell killing. It does not establish that every approved drug affecting this pathway reproduces the result or achieves suitable exposure and selectivity.

## Evidence boundaries

- Specify context and endpoint; distinguish bulk-cell effects, stem-cell effects, and differentiation.
- Approval, original indication, exposure and selectivity facts outside these summaries need explicit verification. Label recollections as unverified prior knowledge.
- Include normal-cell and mechanistic comparators; a pathway link alone is insufficient evidence of efficacy.
- State what would disconfirm the proposed drug–mechanism–context relationship.
- Absence from Co-Scientist's reported positive candidates is not an incorrect-answer label.


Proposed answer (the answer to evaluate):
Atovaquone differentiates salvage-limited, differentiation-blocked cytarabine-residual AML by collapsing ubiquinone-dependent DHODH activity before ATP loss.

Hypothesis and context. In post-cytarabine residual AML with a differentiation block, salvage limitation under physiological pyrimidine availability, and retained oxidative metabolism, atovaquone at a verified unbound exposure is hypothesized to inhibit respiratory complex III, shrink the oxidized ubiquinone pool, and restrict DHODH long enough for fate-tracked myeloid maturation and reduced propagation. The intended mediator is pyrimidine depletion while ATP production stays largely intact. Label indications—Pneumocystis pneumonia treatment and prophylaxis, and atovaquone–proguanil for malaria—plus protein binding above 99.9% and mammalian complex III potency are unverified prior knowledge requiring confirmation before exposure claims.

Supported premises. Cytarabine-resistant cells in the studied models were not consistently enriched for immature quiescent leukemia stem cells; they showed mitochondrial and fatty-acid-oxidation-linked oxidative metabolism, and changing that state changed response [S2]. DHODH inhibition promoted myeloid differentiation and affected disease endpoints in experimental AML [S4]. ROS-low, BCL-2-high quiescent leukemia stem cells are a separate selectivity benchmark [S1]. Venetoclax–azacitidine is the established metabolic comparator [S3]. DHODH dependence and salvage limitation in residual cells are unshown by [S2] and [S4] and stay measured gates. Fatty-acid oxidation is accepted only from orthogonal genetic interruption and 13C-fatty-acid flux, because etomoxir-sensitive respiration is not FAO-specific.

Speculative bridges. Bridge 1 is used only if titration curves separate: partial complex III inhibition may shrink oxidized ubiquinone enough to suppress DHODH before ATP loss inside verified unbound Cmax. Bridge 2: gate-positive blasts mature by longitudinal fate, while matched normal CD34-positive DHODH flux and salvage are measured in parallel so any margin is an outcome. Bridge 3: oxidative metabolism is a complex III entry point [S2], pyrimidine dependence is de novo-versus-salvage flux at physiological nucleoside levels, and [S4] is the differentiation precedent; direct atovaquone–DHODH coupling remains speculative. Oxidized-ubiquinone use by human DHODH, uridine bypass, and respiratory-chain-independent yeast URA1 are unverified prior knowledge. Teriflunomide, the active metabolite of leflunomide (rheumatoid arthritis; teriflunomide approved for relapsing multiple sclerosis; unverified prior knowledge), is the reference DHODH inhibitor.

Preclinical strategy. Before any specimen campaign, Screen A confirms unbound Cmax from primary labels and titrates free atovaquone in a reference AML line for DHODH flux, ubiquinone redox, and ATP production rate. Pyrimidine-before-ATP testing continues only if a free concentration raises dihydroorotate:orotate at least twofold and shifts pyrimidine flux while ATP loss stays under 20%. If those curves overlap, or that free EC50 exceeds verified unbound Cmax by an order of magnitude, the project stops, records kinetic or exposure infeasibility, and leaves specimens unopened. Screen B compares published atovaquone–AML and respiratory-chain–DHODH studies for whether residual-state timing and salvage stratification, rather than drug identity alone, are already described. This packet does not establish novelty. Overlap withdraws the novelty claim; mechanism testing continues only after Screen A passes.

Eligibility on the same specimens is a cytarabine pulse and washout, residual oxygen consumption, and FAO by genetic interruption plus 13C-fatty-acid flux, with baseline CD11b and CD14 each below 20% of genotype-confirmed cells. Salvage limitation, under physiological pyrimidine availability, means that blocking de novo synthesis leaves compensatory salvage unable to maintain UTP; substantial de novo labeling or uridine rescue alone does not establish inadequate salvage. ROS-low leukemia stem cells [S1] and pretreatment bulk blasts are separate arms. Teriflunomide in protein-containing medium must raise dihydroorotate:orotate at least twofold, hold ATP within 20% of vehicle, and lose both nucleotide and maturation effects when uridine is supplied. Maturation counts only with barcoding or equivalent longitudinal fate tracking plus absolute counts of genotype-positive immature and mature cells, showing immature cells acquiring mature markers and an absolute rise in the mature compartment rather than enrichment by selective loss. Enzyme assays must show atovaquone inhibits complex III and spares DHODH, and teriflunomide the reverse. Ubiquinone reduction and the pyrimidine-flux change must appear while ATP loss is still under 20% and before markers move; coincident ATP collapse makes that run uninterpretable. URA1, induced only after the residual state is established, must restore pyrimidines while complex III and ubiquinone inhibition remain, and both uridine and URA1 must first reverse teriflunomide or the arm stops.

Matched cycling normal CD34-positive cells are profiled for DHODH flux and salvage under the same physiological conditions. The therapeutic index is the ratio of free concentrations that meet AML maturation and clonogenic endpoints versus matched normal colony endpoints, reported as an observed result with no preset fold cutoff. After these gates, cytarabine-primed xenografts measure marrow free drug, fate-resolved absolute counts, limiting-dilution initiating-cell frequency, and normal hematopoietic recovery.

Alternatives and falsification. Apparent maturation can reflect preferential loss of immature cells, delayed cytarabine injury, direct DHODH binding, other atovaquone targets, or ATP collapse. The relationship is falsified, even if atovaquone remains cytotoxic, when uridine and URA1 restore pyrimidine pools, leave complex III and ubiquinone inhibition intact, and fate-tracked differentiation plus clonogenic loss still persist, while the same rescues reverse teriflunomide. It is also falsified if no free concentration lowers DHODH flux before the ATP rate, or if matched normal CD34-positive DHODH flux and salvage equal residual AML at the same free exposure.

Limitations. Screen A is the prespecified stop when binding leaves no usable unbound window. Normal progenitors that share complex III and de novo pyrimidine dependence may erase a margin, which the index reports rather than assumes. Differentiation need not clear leukemia durably. [S2] models may differ from clinical marrow, [S4] may not hold across genotypes, and murine pyrimidine metabolism may diverge. Exposure figures, URA1 biochemistry, and prior AML publications require external verification.

Ranked proposal:
Atovaquone differentiates salvage-limited, differentiation-blocked cytarabine-residual AML by collapsing ubiquinone-dependent DHODH activity before ATP loss
